answer_plain: Watering every day with salty water (8 dS/m) gives about 44 % less hydrogen uptake over two weeks than one fresh rain of the same size (from 75 % lower to 95 % higher, so it may go up or down). Almost all of that drop is the daily-watering pattern: fresh water given daily gives about 38 % less. Saltiness itself adds only a few points. A separate crop formula (not the twin) puts alfalfa at about 89 % of normal yield (83 to 93 %). The twin cannot tell (gives no answer) for a single salty rain, even at 2 dS/m, because the salt in the sand water becomes too strong for its formulas.
answer_science: A single 12 mm rain carrying NaCl at 2 dS/m or more concentrates as the soil dries until the pore-water NaCl exceeds 0.1 mol/L, the limit of the ideal-dilute osmotic model; the twin returns no estimate for any draw of this series. Daily brackish irrigation keeps the solution dilute (refusals 0.78 % at 8 dS/m). Relative to the single fresh rain, daily irrigation at 8 dS/m changed uptake by a median of −37 % (90 % interval −75 to +95 %), and daily irrigation with near-fresh water (0.5 dS/m) by −29 % (−72 to +133 %). Salinity therefore adds a few percentage points to an effect set by the irrigation schedule, whose sign depends on the retention curve. With the FAO-29 leaching relation and the Maas–Hoffman response, alfalfa relative yield at 8 dS/m is 89 % (83 to 93 %), a crop-model estimate driven by the twin's salt balance.
baseline_label: One 12 mm fresh rain on day 1, no irrigation

headline_plain: Watering every day with salty water (8 dS/m) gives about 44 % less hydrogen uptake over two weeks than one fresh rain (and may go up or down), but fresh daily watering alone gives about 38 % less.
headline_science: A single 12 mm rain carrying NaCl at 2 dS/m or more concentrates as the soil dries until the pore-water NaCl exceeds 0.1 mol/L, the limit of the ideal-dilute osmotic model; the twin returns no estimate for any draw of this series.
limits_plain: The range shows how much the answer moves when uncertain numbers in the models are varied; the models themselves could also be wrong. When salt concentration in the sand water rises above a tenth of a mole per litre, the twin refuses to guess rather than extrapolate outside its formulas. Crop yields come from published crop-salt formulas, not from the twin.
limits_science: The osmotic model is valid for dilute solutions; the refusal of the saline-rain series marks the boundary of the model, and estimates for concentrated pore water require an activity model. Crop yields come from the FAO-29 and FAO-56 salt-tolerance relations; the twin contributes the soil salt balance of bare sand.
